title: Craft, Commerce, and Jewish Working Life in Będzin
summary: Records of craftsmen, merchants, cooperatives, and labor organizing show that Będzin’s Jewish life was also rooted in work and economic mutual aid.

editorialContent:
![Będzin, the town where Jewish artisans organized their working lives](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/11/B%C4%99dzin_-_Zamek_obronny_z_XIVw..jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)

## Work, skill, and mutual dependence

In Będzin, skilled work was more than a way to earn a living. Tailors, metalworkers, bakers, carpenters, shoemakers, hairdressers and other tradespeople supported households, trained apprentices, and helped sustain the institutions of Jewish communal life. The founding of the [Handwerker Association](/communities/bedzin/records/event_candidate_7755d5f349b987d533bc7a02) gave these workers a shared organization through which they could address common needs and make their presence felt beyond the workshop.

The memorial book places this association within a broader professional movement. Its account of Będzin’s Jewish trade unions traces early organizing to 1905–1906, before the artisans’ association was founded. At that time, according to the book, a master craftsman often settled disputes with an apprentice on his own. The relationship could be close—apprentices might live much like members of the master’s family—but it also left younger workers vulnerable. The account recalls outsiders seeking work who were pressured by local “strong people,” and says that socialist parties and trade organizing helped displace those informal power structures. These are the book’s recollections, not a complete record of every workplace or worker.

Organizing took varied forms. The memorial book describes earlier unions among painters, coachmen and commercial clerks, followed by groups of carpenters, mill workers and others. It recounts a failed campaign by women’s tailors: employers responded to demands with a lockout, and the ensuing breakdown helped prompt the creation of a cooperative. That cooperative soon became private, the book says, and the organization fell apart. The episode shows both the promise and fragility of collective solutions when workers faced employers with greater economic power.

## A club becomes an institution

The memorial book dates the association’s founding to September 1916, initially as an artisans’ club with its own statute. It names H. L. Goldsztajn among the founders, alongside Ch. D. Rudzyn, Sz. Klajner, D. Lustiger, Z. Wajnsztok, H. Jakubowicz, M. Bornsztajn, Sz. Elbaum, A. Bryner, Sz. Inowroclowski, A. Rodzynski, M. Aronowicz, L. Blumenfrucht, Dr. Rotsztajn and others. At its first meeting, on 16 September 1916, the dentist Dr. Rotsztajn was elected chairman; L. Blumenfrucht succeeded him in February 1917.

The book also reports that many artisans initially looked outside their own ranks for a chairman, because they did not yet see how an organization of tradespeople might be led by tradespeople themselves. That detail captures a transition: from work organized through individual master-apprentice relationships toward representation by an institution accountable to its members.

There is, however, a date discrepancy worth preserving. The book says the association was founded in September 1916, but also calls a celebration on 2 February 1927 its tenth anniversary. Those dates do not align exactly. The supplied event record gives September 1916, while the translated chapter identifies the 1927 event as the tenth anniversary. The evidence does not explain the difference, so the two dates should not be forced into a single precise chronology.

## Guilds, loans, and representation

Over time, the association’s role expanded beyond fellowship. The memorial book describes a structure of trade guilds representing distinct occupations, including tailors, metalworkers, carpenters, butchers, bakers, painters and shoemakers. In its account, the guilds together numbered around 100 in metalwork, 80 in carpentry, 50 among butchers and 45 among bakers; the tailors’ guild was much larger, with about 300 members. These figures are the book’s estimates, and they convey the range of work organized under one roof rather than a complete census of Będzin’s artisans.

The association also connected practical aid with professional advancement. It supported courses to prepare Jewish artisans for master-craftsman examinations, helped with the legalization of tradespeople and apprentices, and maintained two funds that offered members loans. Its representatives served in bodies including the labor court, municipal council and communal institutions. H. L. Goldsztajn, known in the supplied records as [H. L. Goldstein](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_9bb935e5efda6aa503ae1504), became a prominent representative; the book says the association was among the city’s respected institutions and that artisans nominated candidates for municipal councils.

The association’s regional links also mattered. The memorial book says Goldsztajn and H. Jakubowicz represented Będzin at a [craftsmen’s conference in Łódź](/communities/bedzin/records/event_candidate_67e9b7f9d168e2affe976527) on 24–25 February 1918. A separate passage describes a regional conference of Jewish leather workers from 16 towns in Kielce Voivodeship. Such meetings suggest that local organization was part of a wider effort to share experience and press occupational concerns, though the surviving account does not detail every resolution or outcome.

## Celebration and renewal

The association’s public standing was visible at its anniversary celebration. On 2 February 1927, a large gathering took place in the Nawaszci cinema hall. The memorial book describes thousands attending, with delegations from Jewish institutions in Zagłębie and farther away, alongside representatives of the government, city council and Jewish community. Goldsztajn was named honorary chairman in recognition of his service.

Yet the same account does not present institutional life as smooth. It says disputes among leaders weakened the association’s authority in members’ eyes. In June 1932, new leaders—including [L. Brama](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_fd2eeb48ff3b2225bb707c56), [M. J. Prachtzweig](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_f98e09fee7694b7a8d198045), [A. Blochaz](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_884a0ede7d59983a0b970c63), and Rudaler—helped revive it, with Goldsztajn again at its head. The book says the association then adopted the statutes of the Central Association in Warsaw and revived its guilds. By 1937, it lists [A. Y. Fershtenfeld](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_666561f1cc729dda53fbbd22) as vice-chairperson among the association’s representatives.

The book’s wider portrait of Będzin’s economy includes merchants and enterprises as well as guild members: [Jacob Gutman’s iron-trading firm](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_8caf82f91c5a95f30b32402a), the Friedrich brothers’ brass foundry, and [Lipa Kanal](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_95d55aee5d349cda603c9a9a), described as a prosperous timber merchant. They were not all members of the Handwerker Association, and the account does not establish that they were. Their stories nevertheless point to the varied economic world in which skilled labor, commerce and family livelihoods intersected.

## What the wider record adds

Independent sources place Będzin’s associations within a town where Jewish life was substantial: the English-language account of Będzin’s history on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C4%99dzin) reports that Jews made up a majority of the population in the 1921 census. That demographic context helps explain why an artisans’ institution could become prominent in municipal and communal affairs. It does not independently confirm the Handwerker Association’s founding date or the details of its internal history.

The later destruction of this working world must also be kept distinct from the association’s own testimony. The [Yad Vashem Encyclopedia of the Ghettos entry for Będzin](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=150) documents the wartime ghetto and persecution of the town’s Jews. The memorial book remembers Jewish labor under occupation, including forced work, in a radically altered economy. Neither source makes the prewar association’s story a simple prelude to the Holocaust: its members’ work, disputes, loans, training and civic representation mattered in their own time. Remembering that everyday collective effort restores one dimension of the community that was later attacked and destroyed.
